we have developed the first artificial agent to learn to excel at a variety of challenging control tasks, using only pixels as inputs, and that this was accomplished using a deep reinforcement learning algorithm that is based on the temporal difference learning rule.

we have developed a new algorithm that is able to learn to play Atari 2600 video games directly from pixels, and that this new algorithm outperforms the performance of all other previously published algorithms.
we have demonstrated that reinforcement learning can be applied successfully to a complex domain in which agents receive raw sensory inputs.

the problem of how an agent may learn to act optimally in complex, uncertain environments, given only a reward function as a performance criterion.
understanding the computational principles of animal intelligence, and developing a theory of reinforcement learning that can be applied to the control of complex agents.
the question of how agents may learn to control an environment.

we have developed a novel deep reinforcement learning architecture that can learn control policies directly from high-dimensional sensory inputs using end-to-end reinforcement learning.

the combination of deep neural networks and reinforcement learning can produce agents that super-humanly excel at many tasks.
